cases.title: Designed a POS notification service with three urgency levels, adopted as the team's standard

tldr.problem: The new POS needed one way to get a cashier's attention, and some notifications need an answer while others don't.
tldr.decision: A hybrid: severity picks the transport (RPC for blocking, pub/sub for inform), and category only sets the look.
tldr.outcome: The team adopted it, adding notification types stayed easy, and later hardware flows like POS reboot reuse it for verification.

cases.teaser: Not every notification deserves an answer.

quiz.question: Some POS notifications need the cashier's answer and some don't. How would you send them between services over MQTT?

options.label: Send everything over pub/sub
options.reply: Fire and forget is simple and fast for a heads-up, but nothing waits for the cashier's answer on the blocking ones.

options.label: Send everything over RPC
options.reply: Right for blocking notifications, but making every heads-up wait for a reply is heavy.

options.label: Let severity pick the transport
options.reply: That's the hybrid we adopted. Blocking notifications go over RPC and wait; informational ones are published. Category only sets the look.

body.title: Context
body.lede: A convenience-store chain was replacing its monolithic point-of-sale system with microservices.

blocks.html: The services talk over MQTT, using both pub/sub and RPC topics. I was a senior developer on a team of about 15, consulting through Momentum3. The system was greenfield, and I designed its notification service.

rows: Conductor
Coordinates a sale and sends notifications to the UI.
Transaction
Owns the sale, and so where it lives.
Hardware
Drives the store hardware.
UI
Shows the notification and collects the cashier's answer.

body.title: Problem
body.lede: Notifications travel between the conductor and the UI, and they don't all behave the same way.

blocks.html: Some events only need a heads-up. Others must stop a single register, and a few must stop the whole POS until someone answers. Those blocking ones need a reply from the cashier, so the sender has to wait for it. The informational ones don’t.

body.title: Options
body.lede: I presented two approaches to the tech leads, split by how a notification moves over MQTT.

items.label: Option A
items.title: Everything over pub/sub
items.body: Fire and forget. Simple and fast for informational messages, but nothing waits for the cashier’s answer.

items.label: Option B
items.title: Everything over RPC
items.body: Every notification waits for a reply. Right for blocking messages, but heavy for a simple heads-up.

body.title: Decision
body.lede: The team adopted a hybrid that separates what a notification does from how it looks.

items: Severity picks the transport. Blocking notifications (block one register, block the whole POS) go over RPC and wait for an answer. Informational ones go over pub/sub.
Category only sets the look, such as color and position on screen.
Because the two are separate, a notification’s look and its behavior can change without touching each other.

blocks.label: What changed later
blocks.title: Position moved from the UI to the backend
body: The plan was for the UI to set where a notification appears. It moved to the backend, because the backend owns where the transaction lives, and that decides where the notification should show.

body.title: Outcome
body.lede: The design held up as the POS grew.

blocks.html: Adding new notification types stayed easy. The same service later carried hardware flows I built, such as POS reboot and stop POS, which use a notification for verification instead of a password.

rows: Split behavior from look.
Severity decides what a notification does and how it travels. Category decides how it looks. Each can change on its own.
Match the transport to the need for an answer.
If someone has to respond, use RPC and wait. If not, publish it and move on.
Be willing to move ownership.
Position started in the UI and moved to the backend once it was clear the backend owned the information it depended on.

cases.title: Redesigned money-order printing so a failed print refunds the customer automatically

tldr.problem: Printing a money order is slow and can fail partway. The old flow waited on the printer and had no clean way back from a failed print.
tldr.decision: Run it as a saga: totaling continues while printing runs asynchronously, and a failed print triggers its own refund transaction.
tldr.outcome: A failed print now refunds the customer automatically, verified on real money-order hardware.

cases.teaser: The time a printer tried to keep a customer's money.

quiz.question: A money order can fail to print after the customer has paid. How would you structure the flow?

options.label: Keep printing inside the transaction and handle failures there
options.reply: It's the smallest change, but the register still blocks while it prints, and every failure still runs through the happy path.

options.label: Split it into steps that each recover on their own
options.reply: I ran it as a saga. Totaling keeps going while printing runs asynchronously, and a failed print triggers its own refund transaction.

body.title: Context
body.lede: A convenience-store chain was replacing its monolithic point-of-sale system with microservices.

blocks.html: The services talk over MQTT. I was a senior developer on a team of about 15, consulting through Momentum3, and I owned money orders end to end, from business rules to printing on real store hardware.

rows: Conductor
Coordinates a sale across the other services.
Transaction
Totals the sale and records each money order.
Hardware
Drives the money-order printer at the counter.
UI
Shows the cashier what happened and what to do next.

body.title: Problem
body.lede: Printing is slow and can fail partway, and the old flow had no clean way back.

blocks.html: Totaling the transaction waited on the printer, so the register sat blocked during every print. When a print failed, the failure tangled with the normal path. In payments, a failure can’t leave the customer charged for a document they never got.

body.title: Options
body.lede: I weighed keeping printing inside the transaction against splitting the flow into steps that each recover on their own.

items.label: Option A
items.title: Keep printing in the transaction
items.body: Simplest to change. The register still blocks while it prints, and every failure still runs through the happy path.

items.label: Option B
items.title: Run it as a saga
items.body: Separate steps, each with its own recovery. More moving parts, but a failed print has one clear place to go.

body.title: Decision
body.lede: I redesigned the flow in the conductor service as a saga.

items: Totaling continues while printing runs asynchronously.
The print timeout scales with the number of documents, so a large order isn’t cut off early.
Failed prints go down their own path and trigger an automatic refund transaction.
A low-document alert warns the store before the printer runs out.

blocks.label: How I proved it
blocks.title: Tests for every path the transaction could take
body: I planned tests for all prints failing (refund, no details recorded), all succeeding, and a mix of two successes and one failure. Others covered the timeout scaling, the timeout expiring with the right exception, and the low-document alert. Then I verified it on real money-order hardware in the store lab.

body.title: Outcome
body.lede: A failed print now refunds the customer automatically, in the same flow.

blocks.html: Money orders were built and verified in the store lab with configurable limits, no refunds after printing, employee-ID verification, and fees as sub-line items. Before I left, they reached a few stores as part of the pilot.
The whole team, including the product owner, signed off on it in a demo. I picked up the saga pattern from the fuel service, and after money orders, the boot-up and checkout flows used it too.

rows: The design question was "what happens when step three fails?"
The saga answers that before anyone asks. Each step knows how to recover, so a failure never falls through to the happy path.
I started with the easiest test, not the hardest.
Writing out every branch first, then testing from the top down, got me unstuck when the hardest test kept stalling.

cases.title: Shipped a user-facing LLM feature: Pocket Log, a bowling analytics app

tldr.problem: League bowlers get a printout of every shot, but the patterns behind their scores stay buried.
tldr.decision: Plain code handles scoring and shot projections. The model only coaches: one pass on the night, one on your overall game.
tldr.outcome: In use on my own league nights. A teammate starts once it's live on the site.

cases.teaser: My league nights, turned into data.
